quote: The Charleston happens at the very start of every hand, before anyone draws or discards.
issue: The page never introduces the term in the bold-term pattern from your voice guide. "Hand" is also doing double duty (one round of play vs. the tiles you hold), which can trip up a beginner in the very first line. See the sitewide note on "hand" below.
suggested_fix: The **Charleston** is a set of tile swaps at the very start of every round, before anyone draws or discards.

quote: You're dealt 13 tiles at random, so most starting hands aren't close to any hand on the card.
issue: "The card" isn't explained anywhere on this page. Your brief says each article should stand alone for someone who lands on it from Google.
suggested_fix: You're dealt 13 tiles at random, so most starting hands aren't close to any hand on the card (the yearly list of winning hands from the National Mah Jongg League).

quote: In the first round, you pass to your right, then across the table, then to your left, and you receive three tiles from the other players each time.
issue: Ambiguous. It reads as if all three players hand you tiles at once. A beginner won't know who is passing to her.
suggested_fix: In the first round, you pass to your right, then across the table, then to your left. Each time you pass, another player passes three tiles to you.

quote: This first round is required.
issue: The rule comes after the details, so the reader learns it last. A small reorder reads more naturally.
suggested_fix: Move it up: "The first round is required. You pass to your right, then across the table, then to your left."

quote: On the last pass, you may pass "blind": you can hand along tiles you just received without looking at them.
issue: "May" sounds a little formal here. Separate question for your rules expert: this sentence sits only in the first-round paragraph, so readers may assume a blind pass isn't allowed in the second round.
suggested_fix: On the last pass, you can pass "blind," which means passing along tiles you just received without looking at them.

quote: If anyone says no, you skip straight to play.
issue: This conflicts with the next paragraph, which describes a courtesy pass after the Charleston. A reader could take it to mean a "no" cancels the courtesy pass too. Rule question for your expert.
suggested_fix: If anyone says no, you skip the second round.

quote: After the Charleston, players sitting across from each other may agree to a courtesy pass, swapping anywhere from zero to three tiles.
issue: "Zero" sounds odd, since you can't swap zero tiles. "Courtesy pass" is new vocabulary and should get the bold-term treatment.
suggested_fix: After that, you and the player across from you can agree to a **courtesy pass**, one last swap of up to three tiles.

quote: You don't have to pass your best tiles — the whole point is to let go of tiles you don't need and hope for something more useful in return.
issue: It answers a worry beginners don't really have, so it reads a bit off. Lead with the advice instead.
suggested_fix: The idea is to let go of tiles you don't need and hope for something more useful in return.

quote: Hang on to pairs and anything that shows up in several hands on the card — those are worth keeping until you're sure you won't need them.
issue: "Hang on to" and "worth keeping" say the same thing. "Pairs" isn't defined on this page.
suggested_fix: Hang on to pairs (two matching tiles) and any tile that shows up in several hands on the card, at least until you're sure you won't need them.

quote: Once passing is done, regular play begins: the dealer discards first, and turns move around the table from there.
issue: Doesn't say which way turns go. The Rules page says counterclockwise; one clause fixes it here.
suggested_fix: Once passing is done, regular play begins. The dealer discards first, and turns move to the right (counterclockwise) from there.

quote: Every hand listed on the NMJL card has a point value printed right next to it — that's what you're playing for.
issue: NMJL isn't spelled out on first use on this page. "That's what you're playing for" is vague (points? money?), and the sentence works without it.
suggested_fix: Every hand on the National Mah Jongg League (NMJL) card has a point value printed next to it.

quote: Check your current card for the exact numbers, since they can change year to year.
issue: Small idiom fix.
suggested_fix: Check your current card for the exact numbers, since they can change from year to year.

quote: Some hands on the card have to be played concealed, which means you haven't exposed any groups.
issue: The tense is off ("haven't" points to the past), and "exposed" isn't defined on this page.
suggested_fix: Some hands must be played **concealed**, which means you keep all your tiles on your rack and don't set any groups face-up on the table.

quote: They are often worth more, but they're harder to complete, since you can't call tiles to speed things along.
issue: Possibly misleading. As I understand it, you can still call the final tile to win with a concealed hand. Not my call; please have your rules expert check. Also, "They are" next to "they're" in the same sentence; your brief favors contractions.
suggested_fix: They're often worth more, but they're harder to complete, since you can't call discards to build them. (Expert to confirm whether to add: "except the tile that wins.")

quote: (section heading) Concealed vs. exposed hands
issue: The section never explains exposed hands, so the "vs." in the heading doesn't pay off.
suggested_fix: Add one sentence after the concealed explanation, e.g. "Hands marked X can include exposed groups." (Expert to confirm the marking.)

quote: (whole paragraph)
issue: Five rules are packed into one paragraph. Your brief asks for short lists for steps like this. Also, "Under the standard rules" and "Your card and your group will tell you which of these apply" pull in opposite directions: is this the standard or isn't it?
suggested_fix:
When someone wins, the other three players pay the winner directly. There's no shared pot. Here's how much each person pays:
- If you threw the tile that completed the winning hand, you pay double. The other two players pay the regular amount.
- If the winner drew the winning tile from the wall, all three players pay double.
- Many hands also pay double if the winner used no jokers.
Some groups add their own house rules, so it's worth asking before you start.

quote: Many hands also pay double when played without any jokers.
issue: Rule question, not wording: readers will wonder whether the doubles stack (for example, no jokers plus a self-drawn tile). Worth one sentence if your expert can confirm.
suggested_fix: (Expert to advise.)

quote: It gets natural fast once you've seen it happen a few times.
issue: "Gets natural fast" isn't idiomatic, and "a few times" repeats from the sentence before.
suggested_fix: After you've seen it a couple of times, it starts to feel natural.

quote: Scoring feels like a lot at first, but most tables are happy to walk you through it the first few times you win or lose a hand.
issue: "Feels like a lot" also opens the Beginner Guide. Fine on its own, but repetitive if someone reads both pages.
suggested_fix: Scoring can seem complicated at first, but most tables are happy to walk you through it the first few times you win or lose a hand.

quote: Charleston: "start of every hand" / Scoring: "When a hand ends" / Terms > Wall Game: "A round that ends..."
issue: "Hand" means both the tiles you hold and one round of play. Experienced players use it both ways, but a beginner reading "the hand isn't quite over" next to "your hand matches the card" may stumble.
suggested_fix: Pick one: use "round" for one deal and "hand" for your tiles, or keep both meanings and define them in Terms.

quote: American Mahjong / Mah Jongg / NMJL / the card
issue: In my earlier note I suggested lowercase "mahjong" per AP. Since your brief and the site name both use "American Mahjong" with a capital M, that's a perfectly good house style. Keep it and just be consistent.
suggested_fix: Term list: "American Mahjong" for the game. "Mah Jongg" only in proper names and program titles (National Mah Jongg League, "Learn to Play Mah Jongg"). Spell out "National Mah Jongg League (NMJL)" on first use on every page. "The card" lowercase in body text; "The Card" is fine as a glossary heading.

quote: open play / guided play
issue: These two terms appear on almost every city page but aren't in the Terms glossary. A newcomer won't know the difference, and it's exactly what decides where she should go first.
suggested_fix:
Add two entries (expert to confirm):
**Open play** — Casual games that anyone who knows the rules can join, usually without a teacher.
**Guided play** — Games with a teacher at or near the table who helps as you go.
As a modifier, keep the hyphen ("open-play socials"), as the intros already do.

quote: Learn: "Bams, Dots, and Craks" / Intros: "Alpharetta, Roswell and Milton"
issue: The Learn guides use the serial comma and the city intros don't. AP drops it; Chicago keeps it.
suggested_fix: If you're going with AP, remove the serial comma from the Learn guides.

quote: Birmingham's listings center on two community sites.
issue: "[City]'s listings center on," "is centered on" and "is built around" open about 13 intros. "Listings" also describes the website rather than the city, which makes the pages sound like a database.
suggested_fix: Vary the openers using the three structures below. Keep "listings" for places where you're being upfront about coverage (New York, San Francisco), where it does real work.

where: City intros > "If you are new" (16 cities)
quote: If you are new, the two-part series is a good place to start.
issue: "If you are new" / "If you're new" appears in 16 intros, with and without the contraction.
suggested_fix: Use the contraction everywhere. Cut the line when the paragraph already makes the beginner option clear, and vary it where you keep it ("If you've never played...", "For a first lesson...").

quote: Check the event pages for the current location and dates before you go.
issue: The same generic advice closes many intros. Readers who browse a few cities will notice it.
suggested_fix: Move it to one sitewide line near the listings, e.g. "Times and places change, so check the event page before you go." Keep only city-specific cautions, which are genuinely useful: Kansas City and Phoenix (confirm the style), Fort Worth (series pricing).

where: City intros > "good first step" etc. (about 11 cities)
quote: If you're new, a beginner lesson is a good first step.
issue: "Good first step," "good fit" and "good place to start" are vague and read like soft endorsements of a business you haven't vetted.
suggested_fix: Say who it's for instead: "made for people who've never played," "for players who know the basics."

where: City intros > Los Angeles, New York, Philadelphia
quote: In Los Angeles, our listings center on two groups...
issue: "Our" and "we" appear in only three or four intros.
suggested_fix: Pick one: a light "we" voice throughout, or none.

where: City intros > Houston, Richmond, Los Angeles, Seattle
quote: Houston Mahjong Club runs an NMJL league...
issue: NMJL isn't spelled out. Each city page is its own landing page.
suggested_fix: "...runs a National Mah Jongg League (NMJL) league..." (or rephrase to avoid "league league": "runs a league that plays by National Mah Jongg League rules")

where: City intros > Memphis, Sacramento, San Francisco
quote: ...teach American Mah Jongg... / ...American Mah Jongg classes... / ...American Mah Jongg social play...
issue: Used in running text, not as a proper name. If these are the programs' actual titles, fine; otherwise use "American Mahjong."
suggested_fix: Check against each listing.

where: City intros > Atlanta (Structure C: learn, then play)
quote: (full paragraph)
issue: Sample rewrite. Opens with what makes the city easy to navigate, then follows the path from lesson to regular play. No closing advice line needed.
suggested_fix: In Atlanta, the same groups that teach beginners also host social play. Le Mahj Club teaches 101 and 102 beginner lessons and hosts casual open-play socials around Alpharetta, Roswell and Milton. In Buckhead, Mahj Studios is a membership club where you can take beginner lessons, try guided play and come back for socials. Several independent instructors also teach American Mahjong across the metro.

where: City intros > Birmingham (Structure B: lead with the place)
quote: (full paragraph)
issue: Sample rewrite. Opens on a concrete venue instead of "listings." I dropped the "check the event pages" closer, assuming it moves to a sitewide line.
suggested_fix: At the Levite Jewish Community Center in Birmingham, open play is free, and a multi-part Mahjong 101 series teaches the basics. In Mountain Brook, O'Neal Library hosts a recurring meetup that plays from the National Mah Jongg League card, with a beginner lesson on the first Monday. Both are set up for newcomers.

where: City intros > Boise (Structure A: start with the newcomer)

suggested_fix: If you're just starting out in Boise, look for the two-part introductory series from Mahjong at the Local. It meets at LOCAL Boise downtown and teaches from the National Mah Jongg League card. If you'd rather learn privately, OK LET'S MAHJONG offers private lessons, and it hosts community events too. Dates and sign-up details are on each event page.

where: City intros > Buffalo (Structure B: lead with the place)
quote: (full paragraph)

where: City intros > Hartford (Structure A: start with the newcomer)
quote: (full paragraph)
issue: Sample rewrite. Keeps the card reminder because it's specific to this venue. Note: the original says to take 101 and then join open studio, so I kept 102 as optional rather than implying it's required first.
suggested_fix: Beginners in the Hartford area can learn the game at a local bookshop. River Bend Bookshop in West Hartford hosts Linda Houde's American Mah Jongg 101 course, and you can join the shop's regular open studio night when you're ready to practice. A 102 intermediate course is there when you want to go further. Bring a current National Mah Jongg League card, since the bookshop's event pages ask for one. Those pages also list the next course dates.
